synopsis: Comparable heavy off-road braking functions historically took three to four years to validate, largely through physical testing and tuning for each machine model; off-road validation remains more physical than automotive practice, with immature test infrastructure [f282, f11919, f1243, f344]. The recommended approach retains physical testing but reserves proving-ground and field work for calibration, simulator qualification, coupled behavior and final high-risk cases, using real machines to confirm stopping, terrain and environmental effects [f4110, f7669, f551]. Physical targets provide an end-to-end reality anchor, but level-track success can conceal grade-related trigger errors, and staged-target track tests cannot measure nuisance braking, which requires real operations [f5345, f6350, f11767]. Physical tests also remain part of acceptance frameworks: ISO 17757:2019 uses physical braking and steering tests, while Euro NCAP’s 2026 virtual-testing protocol requires random physical verification and rejects a cluster dossier below a 75% verification-test pass threshold [f7734, f1216, f2513]. A program starting in October 2026 could realistically have a proving-ground kit working by mid-2027, but unexamined booking lead times, capacity and machine suitability create a planning gap; post-prototype work should correlate models, rerun trusted scenarios, confirm worst cases on track and run shadow mode [f68, f5120, f11342].
